title: ACA stroke (distal to ACom): contralateral leg deficit + incontinence
topic: Anterior cerebral artery stroke / circle of Willis
vignette: A 58-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to a 3-hour history of abrupt-onset weakness and numbness of the right lower extremity, as well as urinary incontinence. Two months ago, the patient was hospitalized due to left-sided weakness that resolved spontaneously after several hours. At that time, MRI of the head and MR angiography of the head and neck were normal, but the patient was found to have atrial fibrillation. An oral anticoagulant was prescribed at discharge, but the patient has been nonadherent with therapy. Blood pressure is 162/94 mm Hg and pulse is 102/min and irregularly irregular. Physical examination shows weakness and sensory loss in the right lower extremity. Babinski sign is present on the right. Speech is normal. Examination of the right upper extremity and the left extremities is unremarkable. An embolic occlusion affecting which of the following vascular regions is the most likely cause of this patient's current symptoms?

clues.text: weakness and numbness of the right lower extremity
clues.note: Motor and sensory deficits of the contralateral LEG (with the arm/face spared) localize to the medial motor/sensory cortex - anterior cerebral artery territory (leg area of the homunculus).
Urinary incontinence (loss of cortical inhibition of the micturition center in the medial frontal lobe) is characteristic of an anterior cerebral artery stroke.
Atrial fibrillation (with nonadherence to anticoagulation) is a source of cardioembolism causing embolic stroke.

clues.text: Examination of the right upper extremity and the left extremities is unremarkable
clues.note: Sparing of the arm and face (only the leg affected) points away from the middle cerebral artery and toward the anterior cerebral artery.

whatMatters: Contralateral LEG weakness/sensory loss (arm and face spared) plus urinary incontinence = ANTERIOR CEREBRAL ARTERY (ACA) stroke (medial frontal/parietal cortex). For symptoms to occur, the embolus must lodge DISTAL to the anterior communicating artery (ACom) - proximal to it, the circle of Willis provides collateral flow. Answer A.
strategy: Localize the deficit to the ACA (leg > arm/face, incontinence), then use the circle of Willis logic: an occlusion PROXIMAL to the ACom can be bypassed by collateral flow (often asymptomatic), so a SYMPTOMATIC ACA stroke is usually DISTAL to the ACom. Reject ACA proximal to ACom (collateralized), and MCA branches (superior division -> face/arm + Broca aphasia; inferior division -> Wernicke aphasia/visual; MCA stem -> global deficits) which cause arm/face/language deficits, not an isolated leg deficit.

options.text: Anterior cerebral artery distal to the origin of the anterior communicating artery
Anterior cerebral artery proximal to the origin of the anterior communicating artery
Inferior division of the middle cerebral artery
Superior division of the middle cerebral artery
Trunk of the middle cerebral artery before the bifurcation

eliminations.label: ACA proximal to ACom - collateralized (often asymptomatic)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an occlusion of the A1 segment BEFORE the anterior communicating artery. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the ACom provides collateral flow from the opposite side, so a proximal occlusion is often asymptomatic; a symptomatic ACA stroke is usually DISTAL to the ACom. ✅ Correct if: asking which location is protected by collateral flow.

eliminations.label: Inferior division of MCA - Wernicke aphasia/visual, not leg
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: supplies lateral temporal/parietal cortex. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it causes sensory deficits of the face/arm, visual field defects, and Wernicke (receptive) aphasia/hemineglect - not an isolated leg deficit. ✅ Correct if: fluent aphasia + visual field cut with face/arm sensory loss.

eliminations.label: Superior division of MCA - face/arm + Broca aphasia (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: supplies the lateral frontal cortex. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it causes contralateral FACE and ARM weakness with Broca (expressive) aphasia - the arm/face are spared here and speech is normal, so it's ACA, not MCA. ✅ Correct if: face/arm weakness + non-fluent aphasia.

eliminations.label: MCA trunk (stem) - global hemispheric deficit
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: proximal MCA occlusion affecting the entire MCA territory. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it produces profound contralateral face/arm (> leg) hemiparesis, hemianesthesia, global aphasia, and gaze deviation - far more than this isolated leg deficit. ✅ Correct if: massive MCA-territory stroke.

reasoning: Contralateral LEG weakness/sensory loss + urinary incontinence, arm/face spared = anterior cerebral artery stroke
The circle of Willis (via the anterior communicating artery) collateralizes proximal ACA occlusions
So a symptomatic ACA infarct must be DISTAL to the anterior communicating artery (no collateral)
-> ACA distal to the origin of the ACom; answer A
mechanism: The ANTERIOR CEREBRAL ARTERY (ACA) supplies the MEDIAL surfaces of the frontal and parietal lobes - the cortical representation of the contralateral LOWER extremity (medial homunculus) and the frontal micturition center. An ACA stroke therefore causes contralateral LEG motor and sensory deficits (with relative sparing of the arm and face) and URINARY INCONTINENCE (loss of cortical inhibition of micturition); a positive Babinski indicates upper-motor-neuron injury. Emboli (here from atrial fibrillation with nonadherent anticoagulation) are a common cause. The CIRCLE OF WILLIS provides collateral protection: the ANTERIOR COMMUNICATING ARTERY (ACom) connects the two ACAs, so an occlusion PROXIMAL to the ACom (A1 segment) can be bypassed by flow from the contralateral side and is often asymptomatic; a SYMPTOMATIC ACA infarct usually results from occlusion DISTAL to the ACom (A2 and beyond), where no collateral exists. Thus the lesion is in the ACA distal to the ACom. Middle cerebral artery occlusions (superior division, inferior division, or stem) instead cause face/arm-predominant deficits with aphasia or neglect - not the isolated leg findings seen here.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Neuro > ACA stroke: contralateral LEG > arm/face weakness/sensory loss + urinary incontinence (medial frontal/parietal cortex); circle of Willis - ACom collateralizes proximal ACA occlusions.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Isolated leg deficit + incontinence = ACA; must be distal to ACom (proximal is collateralized).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on anterior cerebral artery, homunculus, anterior communicating artery, circle of Willis, or micturition center? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: MCA divisions/stem cause face/arm + aphasia/neglect; ACA proximal to ACom is collateralized (often asymptomatic).

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: ACA = contralateral leg deficit + incontinence; symptomatic ACA stroke usually distal to ACom (no collateral).

keywords.front: Contralateral leg weakness + urinary incontinence, arm/face spared
Why symptomatic ACA stroke is distal to ACom

keywords.back: Wernicke aphasia, visual field defect, hemineglect

firstAid.detail: Neuro: contralateral leg deficit + incontinence; lesion distal to ACom.
Neuro > MCA (face/arm, aphasia), ACA (leg); circle of Willis collateral.
Neuro > atrial fibrillation -> embolic stroke; anticoagulate.

memoryHook: ACA feeds the medial 'leg' strip and the pee-control center - so its stroke drops the opposite leg and lets the bladder go; symptoms only show if the clot is past the ACom bridge.
